headline: North Rip Turns Cold and Green — Bonito Beat the Calendar to the Island
subhead: The water changed color before the bonito showed, and by midweek the rips were full of them — bass and blues are still working on their own schedule.
body_markdown:
You feel it before you see it out here. Sometime around Wednesday the wind swung out of the northeast for half a day, just long enough to push a clean, cold ribbon of water up against the Southwest Ledge, and the color went from that flat late-August green to something with more blue in it. That's usually the tell. Within 48 hours the bonito showed, and they showed in numbers — we flagged this exact move last week, said the warm water and building bait density would bring them in on schedule, and here they are, stacked on the north side of the Ledge and working the rip off North Light on the last of the ebb.

The bigger picture: the Sound to our west is still carrying real heat — Kings Point up around 71, New London a touch cooler at 69 — and that gradient is exactly what funnels bait and predators toward the island. Block Island sits right where that warm coastal water collides with the cleaner, better-oxygenated flow coming off the ledges and rips, and that collision is the whole reason this place fishes different than the beaches on either side of us. Bass and bluefish don't need to gamble on murky bay water here — they've got current, cold pockets, and bait getting squeezed into a smaller piece of real estate. That's the draw, every August, without fail.

Stripers are in what I'd call a holding pattern right now, and that's an honest read, not a sales pitch. There are fish on the Southwest Ledge and working the deeper edge of the North Rip, but they're not stacked the way they will be once the moon builds toward full over the next week and a half and the bunker schools in Narragansett Bay and up toward Newport get squeezed tighter. Right now the better bass are coming on live eels fished slow along the boulder fields on the Ledge during the last two hours of the incoming, and on bunker chunks anchored up in the rip on North Rip during a hard ebb. Nothing enormous reported this week — mostly mid-20s to low-30-inch fish, with a handful of upper-30s taken on umbrella rigs trolled tight to the bottom contour where the Ledge drops from 20 feet down into the 40s. If you want a shot at something heavier, that's still a nighttime program — dark, moving water, big profile bait, patience.

Bluefish have been the most dependable fish in the water this week, and that tracks with what bunker density usually does for them — where the bait balls up, the blues show up right behind it. Boats working bunker schools off Point Judith and along the Narragansett shoreline have had steady action on diamond jigs and bucktails, some fish pushing into the 8- to 10-pound class. Chunking has worked just as well as jigging when the schools sit still on the tide change — cut bunker on a fish-finder rig, fished on bottom in 25 to 35 feet, has been picking off the bigger blues while the smaller ones stay up top hammering topwater plugs.

Bonito are the story of the week, and they're behaving the way they always do this time of year — fast, aggressive, and completely uninterested in anything that doesn't match the tiny bait they're keyed on. Half-ounce epoxy jigs and small metal — Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters in silver or green mackerel pattern — worked with a fast, erratic retrieve through the surface froth on the Southwest Ledge has been the ticket. Timing matters more than location right now: the window is short, usually the last two hours of the ebb when current compresses the bait against the ledge structure, and it can shut off as quick as it turns on. Fly guys working small Deceivers and Bonito Bunny patterns on intermediate lines have had good mornings when the wind lays down enough to see the nervous water.

Fluke have softened up, which is the normal late-August pattern and not a red flag. Boats working the channel edges around the Great Salt Pond entrance and the deeper structure off Old Harbor are still picking through legal fish on white Gulp paired with 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the last of the outgoing when the water's moving but not ripping. Expect this to hold through most of September before the real push offshore starts.

Looking ahead, the next few days should keep building on what we're already seeing. If the water stays clean and that northeast breeze keeps nudging cooler water up against the Ledge, the bonito bite should hold or even improve, and false albacore won't be far behind — the pattern almost always follows that sequence once bonito are established this early. The moon is working toward full over the next week to ten days, which is the real trigger to watch for the bass — once that bunker in Narragansett Bay and along the Point Judith shoreline gets squeezed by tide and moon together, that's when the Ledge and the Rip start producing the kind of blitz mornings this island is known for. Until then, work the tide changes, keep the boat quiet on the drift, and don't be surprised if the best fish of the day comes in the last twenty minutes of light.
